questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What a memo has to fix at the top
questions.learningObjective: judge which part of a memo header carries least of the reader's burden
questions.stem: An internal memo opens: 'To: the site team. From: the planning office. Date: 14 March. Subject: the north path.' What has the header left the reader to work out?

options.text: What the memo wants from the reader, since the subject names no action
Who has sent the memo, since a department is given and not a person
options.misconception: treats a sending office as a defect, when the sender of an office memo is the office

options.text: When the memo has to be acted on, since the date is the day it was written
options.misconception: reads the send date as a deadline, which a header date is not

options.text: Which site is concerned, since the path is named without any reference code
options.misconception: asks for a code, when a place name already identifies the path

questions.explanation: A memo header exists to let a reader triage without reading the body, and the four parts do different amounts of that work. A sending office is a normal way to identify who wrote it, a date on a memo is the day of writing rather than a deadline, and a path named by name is enough for anyone who works on the site. The subject line is the part that travels furthest into the reader's filing system, and north path tells a reader which matter the memo concerns but not whether they are being asked to decide, to inform, or to act. That is the burden the header has pushed onto the first line of the body.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the header appears in the reader's index when the memo is filed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A subject line that names the action
questions.learningObjective: judge what a subject line must carry for the matter to be actionable

stimulus.body: Subject: North path closure. Since the path will be closed for six weeks from 2 June, the diversion via the field gate will not be available. Please note.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A memo reads: 'Subject: North path closure. Since the path will be closed for six weeks from 2 June, the diversion via the field gate will not be available. Please note.' What does its subject line fail to do?

options.text: Fit the space available, since a subject line longer than a line will be cut in the listing
options.misconception: judges the line by its length, when the fault is what it fails to name

options.text: Name the action wanted, so a reader can tell from the subject whether to decide or only read
Avoid repeating the first line of the body, since the two say the same thing twice
options.misconception: objects to a repetition that is the whole purpose of a subject line

options.text: Carry the date that the body supplies, since a line with a date in it is found more easily
options.misconception: invents a disagreement; the body adds the date and the line does not contradict it

questions.explanation: North path closure names a matter and nothing else, and a subject line's job is to let a reader decide from the line alone whether the memo concerns them and what kind of response it expects. Here the line could equally head a memo announcing the closure, one reporting that it has happened, and one asking the site team to find a replacement route, and the three call for different actions. The body does not ask for anything, which is a separate matter; but even a body that asked would leave the line unable to distinguish the three. Length, repetition of the opening line, and the presence of a date are all matters of house style rather than of what the reader can do with the memo.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can tell from the subject line without opening the memo.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The request buried at the end
questions.learningObjective: judge what the position of a request does to the reader's response

stimulus.body: Since the drainage survey is now complete, I am writing to set out what was found. The survey covered the whole catchment above the culvert, and the water that flooded the path in February came from the field drains rather than from the culvert itself. The contractor's report is attached. I would be grateful if the committee could confirm by the end of the month whether the works will go ahead this year, as the contractor's slot is held until then.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A memo runs: 'Since the drainage survey is now complete, I am writing to set out what was found. The survey covered the whole catchment above the culvert, and the water that flooded the path in February came from the field drains rather than from the culvert itself. The contractor's report is attached. I would be grateful if the committee could confirm by the end of the month whether the works will go ahead this year, as the contractor's slot is held until then.' What has the arrangement of this memo done?

options.text: Nothing, since the opening names the survey and a careful reader expects a request at the end
options.misconception: concedes the point to be decided, which is what a reader who skims will do

options.text: Nothing, since the request names the committee, the decision and the date all three
options.misconception: credits the request with clarity, when its position is what is in question

options.text: The request is in the last sentence, so a reader may file the memo as news
It overstates the case, since it asks a committee to settle what a contractor is holding open
options.misconception: objects to the substance, which the passage gives as the reason for writing

questions.explanation: The memo's first sentence sets a genre for the reader: the survey is complete and this sets out what was found, which is the announcement of a finished piece of work. Three sentences of findings follow, and only the last asks anything. A reader who takes the opening as the memo's shape, which most readers do with a long attachment, has a document that reports rather than asks, and files it accordingly; the request is then read, if at all, as a courtesy at the end. The request's own wording is careful, naming the committee, the decision and the date, so the cost of the arrangement is not ambiguity but misfiling.
questions.hint: Ask what genre the first sentence sets, and what a reader does with a memo of that genre.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A subject line that could carry two answers
questions.learningObjective: find the ambiguity in a subject line and name what would remove it
questions.stem: A memo's subject line reads: 'Review of the gate replacement'. What is the reader left unable to tell from it?

options.text: Who carried out the review, since the line names no author and no body
options.misconception: asks for an author, which a subject line has never carried

options.text: How long the review took, since the line gives neither dates nor a duration
options.misconception: asks for duration, which belongs in the body of a memo

options.text: Whether the review has finished, since the line uses no past tense of any kind
options.misconception: reads a grammatical tense as a status report, which is the ambiguity itself

options.text: Whether the memo seeks agreement to a review or reports that a review has happened

questions.explanation: A subject line built from a noun phrase, review of the gate replacement, names an object of thought without saying what has been done with it. The same line can head a memo that asks the committee to approve a review, one that reports a review already done, and one that sets out options for a review; all three are plausible and the line does not choose between them. Naming an author, a duration, or a completion would each answer a question the reader is unlikely to be asking of a subject line. What the line has to do is use the grammar of action, request for approval, completed review, so the reader knows the status before opening it.
questions.hint: Ask what three different memos this one line could head.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What a reader of a status report wants first
questions.learningObjective: identify the judgement a report leaves its reader to make unaided
questions.stem: A one-page weekly report opens: 'This week the team completed the survey, held two meetings, and began the drawings. The drawings are 40 per cent complete. Next week the team will continue.' What does the opening leave a reader to work out?

options.text: Whether the work is on or behind, since no line of the opening gives the state
Who did the work, since the report names a team and not the people inside it
options.misconception: asks for a roster, which a one-page report is not obliged to carry

options.text: What the work has cost, since the report gives a percentage and no money at all
options.misconception: asks for a budget line that this report's purpose does not include

options.text: What happens after next week, since the report stops at a single week ahead
options.misconception: objects to the horizon of a weekly report, which is a week

questions.explanation: A status report is read by someone who did not do the work and has to decide whether to intervene, and the first thing that reader needs is a state, on track, at risk, or behind. This opening lists three completed or started activities and then a percentage, and none of those is a state: work begun this week is neither on track nor behind until it is measured against a plan, and forty per cent means nothing without the figure it started from. A roster and a cost belong in a longer document, and stopping at next week is what a weekly report is for. The judgement the reader is left to make is the one the report exists to supply.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would do differently depending on the answer, and whether the report gives it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A number in a brief with no base
questions.learningObjective: judge what two figures need before they can be compared

stimulus.body: Complaints about the noise from the yard have risen by 60 per cent this quarter. The number of complaints is now 18. Site staff report that late deliveries are the main cause.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A brief to the committee reads: 'Complaints about the noise from the yard have risen by 60 per cent this quarter. The number of complaints is now 18. Site staff report that late deliveries are the main cause.' What can a reader not do with those figures?

options.text: Accept the cause, since site staff hear the yard every day and their report is direct evidence
options.misconception: takes a reported cause as settled, when the open item is the arithmetic

options.text: Check the two figures against each other, since the earlier number behind the rise is not given
Date the quarter, since the brief says this quarter without naming the months
options.misconception: asks for calendar dates, which a brief may leave to the reader

options.text: Choose an action, since the brief ends with a cause and no recommendation
options.misconception: asks for a recommendation that a reporting brief does not promise

questions.explanation: Two figures that describe the same quantity have to be able to live in the same sentence, and these two cannot be tested. If the count is now 18 and the rise is 60 per cent, the earlier count would have been 18 divided by 1.6, which is 11.25, and complaints are counted in whole numbers, so at least one of the two figures is rounded or wrong. The brief never says which, and a reader has no way to find out from the brief. That is what a percentage needs and does not get here: the earlier figure it is a percentage of. The cause and the action are both outside what the figures can settle.
questions.hint: Ask what the 60 per cent is a percentage of, and whether the other figure could be that base.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Figures that count different things
questions.learningObjective: report what two documents' figures have between them

stimulus.body: Report to the committee: The scheme as designed will serve 340 households. Response to the consultation paper: The scheme is expected to benefit about 500 households once the second phase is built.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: Two documents say: 'Report to the committee: The scheme as designed will serve 340 households. Response to the consultation paper: The scheme is expected to benefit about 500 households once the second phase is built.' A member wants to quote one of these figures in a public statement. What must the member settle first?

options.text: Which figure is the later one, since the newer document should carry the newer figure
options.misconception: supplies a recency rule that neither document states anywhere in its text

options.text: Nothing, since the two documents agree on what the scheme will do for residents
options.misconception: collapses two counts that the passages keep deliberately distinct

options.text: Which scheme each figure describes, since one names the scheme as designed and one adds a phase
Whether a household is counted the same way in both, since that is what makes figures comparable
options.misconception: asks the reader to settle a rule the two documents never state, when the gap is which scheme is counted

questions.explanation: The report counts the scheme as designed, which is the first phase, and the consultation response counts the scheme once the second phase is built, which is a larger thing. Both numbers can be correct and a member who quotes either without saying which is quoting something the documents do not stand behind: 340 understates what the response promises, and 500 promises a phase the report does not cover. That is a change of base between two documents rather than a contradiction, and a reader has to settle it before quoting anything. Whether one document is newer, and whether a household is counted alike, are both things a reader may reasonably want to know, and neither is what stands between the two figures.
questions.hint: Ask what each figure counts, not how large it is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The agent a status update removes
questions.learningObjective: judge what a passive status update costs its reader
questions.practice: voice repair in a status update

stimulus.body: The gate has been replaced, the path resurfaced, and the drainage inspected. A delay to the surfacing was expected. The path is due to reopen on 14 June, and the gate will be locked outside opening hours.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A site update to residents reads: 'The gate has been replaced, the path resurfaced, and the drainage inspected. A delay to the surfacing was expected. The path is due to reopen on 14 June, and the gate will be locked outside opening hours.' What has the update's voice cost the reader?

options.text: The dating is missing, since the update says due without saying when it was sent out
options.misconception: asks for a send date, which a dated circular would carry outside the quoted text

options.text: The weight is wrong, since a delay deserves more space in an update to residents
options.misconception: judges emphasis, when what the update lacks is an agent

options.text: The tenses are mixed, since the update opens with finished work and closes with a plan
options.misconception: objects to a structure that a status update is built on

options.text: Nobody is named as responsible, so a reader cannot tell who to ask about it

questions.explanation: Every sentence in the update is built on a form that removes the doer: the gate has been replaced, a delay was expected, the path is due to reopen. A resident reading it learns what the state of the path is and cannot learn who to ask, about the delay or the date, or who decided the gate will now be locked outside opening hours. That last change is a decision someone took, and the update reports it as though it were a property of the gate. Tidy prose in a circular is a defensible house style; what it costs here is the one thing a reader with a complaint needs, which is a person to write to.
questions.hint: Ask which person a reader would name if they wanted to query the delay.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What a recommendation has to say
questions.learningObjective: identify the element a recommendation still lacks and repair it

stimulus.body: I recommend that the committee adopt option 2, the replacement scheme, at an estimated cost of 48,000. It is the cheapest of the three and it can be done inside the current financial year. The other options either exceed the year or require a second tender.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A brief to a committee runs: 'I recommend that the committee adopt option 2, the replacement scheme, at an estimated cost of 48,000. It is the cheapest of the three and it can be done inside the current financial year. The other options either exceed the year or require a second tender.' First name what the recommendation still leaves out, then choose the repair.

options.text: What follows if the committee declines, so the repair adds that and keeps the cost
How the estimate was reached, so the repair should add a breakdown of the 48,000
options.misconception: demands an itemisation that recommending rather than costing does not require

options.text: Which option came second, so the repair should name the runner-up alongside it
options.misconception: asks for a ranking the passage does not need in order to recommend

options.text: Who would carry out the work, so the repair should name the contractor in advance
options.misconception: asks for an appointment the passage properly leaves to the committee

questions.explanation: A recommendation is a decision the reader is being asked to take, and a decision needs the two sides of the weighing: what happens if it is taken and what happens if it is not. The brief gives the first, the cost and the fit with the year, and it disposes of the rejected options, but a committee that declines is left with no statement of the consequence, and the only hint is a contractor's slot, which appears in a different document. Adding one sentence supplies it and leaves the recommendation intact. An itemised estimate belongs to a costing note, a ranking of the rejected options is not needed to recommend one, and naming a contractor pre-empts a decision the committee has not taken.
questions.hint: Ask what a committee is weighing against what it is being asked to choose.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The moves a one-page brief needs
questions.learningObjective: order the elements that make a one-page brief usable in a long meeting
questions.stem: A writer must fit a recommendation about the path scheme onto one page for a committee that will read forty of them. Put the four moves in the order the page needs.

options.text: The cost, because a committee cannot weigh an option it has not been given a price for
What follows if the decision is deferred, so the reader can weigh waiting against acting
The basis of the choice, so the price can be checked against the options rejected
The decision being asked for, so a reader who reads nothing else knows what is on the table

questions.explanation: One page read among forty is read for the decision, so the decision has to be on it and has to be first. The cost comes next because a committee cannot weigh a proposal it has not been priced for, and a recommendation without a figure reads as an assertion. The basis then explains that figure, because a price only means something next to the reason the option chosen is the cheapest and the reason the others were not. The consequence of deferral comes last, and it is the move most often dropped: it is the sentence that lets a member who is minded to wait decide, rather than the sentence that lets a member who is minded to act proceed without thinking. Order the consequence before the price and the reader is asked to weigh something they have not been told the cost of.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs to know to decide, to weigh, to check, and to judge waiting.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Options that leave a third one out
questions.learningObjective: recognise a choice between two options that is not a choice at all

stimulus.body: Two options were put to the committee: replace the fence now, or leave it and monitor. Replacing now costs 14,000 and can be done in the spring. Leaving costs nothing this year.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A brief runs: 'Two options were put to the committee: replace the fence now, or leave it and monitor. Replacing now costs 14,000 and can be done in the spring. Leaving costs nothing this year.' What has the brief done to the decision?

options.text: It has confused the reader, since no option is recommended and a committee needs advice
options.misconception: objects to the absence of a recommendation, which is not what the stem reports

options.text: It has favoured the dearer option, since 14,000 is named and nothing is named for leaving
options.misconception: reads a figure for one option as a preference for it, when both are priced

options.text: It has priced two courses and passed over repairing, the option a member would raise
It has hidden the cost, since 14,000 appears without saying who is asked to pay
options.misconception: asks for a funding source that the passage is not about

questions.explanation: A choice between two courses is a real choice only if those are the plausible courses, and a reader who has watched a fence deteriorate will want to raise a third: patch the failing posts. The brief prices replacement and inaction and never mentions the middle course, so a member who wants to spend something cannot do so from the page, and the decision is narrower than the question. That is a false pair made by what was left out, not by anything the sentences assert. The other three readings attribute positions the passage does not take: it recommends nothing, it prices both courses it names, and it is not about funding.
questions.hint: Ask what a member would say at the meeting that neither printed option answers.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The criterion that does the choosing
questions.learningObjective: identify the measure that turns a list of options into a choice
questions.stem: A brief compares three suppliers on price, on lead time, and on the length of the guarantee. It then says: 'On balance we recommend the second supplier.' What has the brief not supplied?

options.text: The three prices, since a brief that compares must set out what it compared
options.misconception: assumes the figures are absent, when the gap is the step after the comparison

options.text: The name of the second supplier, since a recommendation must say whom it names
options.misconception: asks for a name the stem supplies by position rather than by name

options.text: The length of the guarantee, since it is listed as a measure but never weighed
options.misconception: sees one listed measure as unweighed, which is the general gap asked once

options.text: The weight given to each measure, since without it the choice is one preference

questions.explanation: Three measures and three suppliers give a reader a page of facts and no way to combine them, because combining is a matter of weights: is a week of lead time worth more than a thousand pounds, and how much of a guarantee counts for anything. On balance says the combining happened and does not show it, so a reader who would weigh the measures differently reaches a different supplier from the same page and cannot see where the two readings part. Missing figures would be a different fault, the second supplier is identified by its position, and the guarantee being listed without a value is one instance of the absence of any weighting at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs in order to disagree with the recommendation on stated grounds.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Weighing two options in a memo
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a memo's comparison is a weighing or a summary

stimulus.body: Option 1 costs 9,000 and takes six weeks. Option 2 costs 4,000 and takes two weeks, but the guarantee is two years rather than five. Option 1 finishes before the school term; option 2 finishes after it.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A memo compares two repairs: 'Option 1 costs 9,000 and takes six weeks. Option 2 costs 4,000 and takes two weeks, but the guarantee is two years rather than five. Option 1 finishes before the school term; option 2 finishes after it.' What has the memo not done?

options.text: Said which difference matters, so the reader has the facts and no way to rank them
Costed both options, since only the cheaper one has been given a figure and a time
options.misconception: misses that both options carry a cost and a duration

options.text: Explained the guarantees, since two years and five years mean nothing to a reader
options.misconception: dismisses a stated measure instead of noticing that none is weighed

options.text: Recommended an option, since a memo that leaves the choice open wastes a reader's time
options.misconception: objects to a brief's neutrality, which the passage maintains throughout

questions.explanation: Three sentences, four measures, two options, and every figure supplied: cost, duration, guarantee, and the term each would finish in. What none of it supplies is any statement about how the measures rank against one another, so a reader who cannot close the path for two weeks because the school term is immovable has a different answer from a reader who cannot commit 9,000. That is a summary of two options set side by side, which is a table in sentences, not a weighing of them. Both options are costed, the guarantees are given in the same unit, and a memo may fairly leave the choice to the committee; calling the result a comparison while leaving the ordering unstated is the gap.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to rank the two options for themselves.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A benefit and a cost in different units
questions.learningObjective: judge whether two figures can be added, compared, or traded
questions.stem: A proposal says: 'The change will save about 2,000 a year and will take roughly 60 hours of an officer's time each year.' What can a reader not do with that sentence?

options.text: Say what an hour of that time is worth, since the sentence gives hours and no rate
options.misconception: asks for a rate, when the missing thing is any exchange between the two units

options.text: Say whether the saving outweighs the time, since money and hours are on no one scale
Say whether 2,000 a year is a large sum, since a reader can weigh it against a budget
options.misconception: calls a figure unusable, when it is only the comparison that is blocked

options.text: Say whether the change is affordable, since the sentence prices a saving and no outlay
options.misconception: asks for an outlay the sentence never claims to carry

questions.explanation: A saving and a time are two different quantities, and saying whether one outweighs the other requires an exchange rate between them, which the sentence does not give and the reader is left to invent. Whichever rate a reader supplies decides the answer, and the rate is the most contestable thing in the proposal, which is why leaving it to the reader hides the decision inside an apparently neutral sentence. The hedged figures, about and roughly, add a second layer of the same problem. A single figure can still be judged large or small, and the sentence makes no claim about an outlay, so affordability is a question the proposal has not pretended to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be supplied before money and hours can be added or traded.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Bad news placed first
questions.learningObjective: judge the effect of putting a decision in a message's first sentence

stimulus.body: The funding for the evening class has been cut, so the class will not run this term. Sixty-two people are enrolled and none of them has been told yet. I have held the hall until Friday and the tutor is available either way.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A memo to a class committee reads: 'The funding for the evening class has been cut, so the class will not run this term. Sixty-two people are enrolled and none of them has been told yet. I have held the hall until Friday and the tutor is available either way.' What has the opening done?

options.text: It has softened nothing, since news of a cut should be softened before it is given
options.misconception: makes tone the criterion, when what the stem reports is position

options.text: It has buried the number affected, since 62 waits until the second sentence
options.misconception: calls the second sentence a hiding place

options.text: It puts the decision first, so a reader can act on one line and be right
It has left the reader with nothing to do, since no sentence names an action to take
options.misconception: asks for a recommendation the memo does supply, namely telling the sixty-two

questions.explanation: A reader who takes the first sentence and has to act on it, because the term has begun and the hall is held only until Friday, can act: the class is not running. Nothing later in the memo reverses that, and the two sentences that follow supply what the decision costs, sixty-two people, and the two things still in the writer's hands, a held hall and an available tutor. That is the argument for putting a decision early: it front-loads the part that changes what a reader does and lets the rest of the message be read as detail. The number is one line away, not buried, and softening is a matter of wording rather than of position.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who reads only the first line now knows that they did not know before.

questions.stem: A memo to a class committee reads: 'The hall is booked until Friday and the tutor can do either week. Sixty-two people are enrolled, which is the highest since the class began. I have to tell you that the funding has been cut and the class will not run this term.' What has the arrangement done?

options.text: Nothing, since the news is clearly stated and it sits in the same paragraph
options.misconception: credits completeness with effect, when the item is the reader's route through

options.text: The order is courteous, since good news before bad is the convention in a memo
options.misconception: invents a convention and defends the order as politeness

options.text: The cut should have come first, since bad news is best delivered in writing

questions.learningObjective: judge whether a reply has answered the question it was sent

questions.stem: A reply reads: 'Your question was whether the fence would be replaced this year. The fence has been inspected and found to be safe, and the inspection report is attached. I am sorry for the delay in replying.' What has the reply done?

options.text: It has been discourteous, since the reply opens with a finding and not with the question
options.misconception: judges tone, when the reply's content answers a different question

options.text: It has reported the fence's condition instead of the decision about replacing it

options.misconception: calls a different answer a refusal; it does answer, but not the question

What the writer knows that is written down nowhere else, so it does not leave with them

The action comes last, since it is what turns a record into work and cannot be written until the decision and its conditions are settled.

options.text: A reason for writing to that councillor, since the letter names no ward or division
options.misconception: asks for a routing detail, which the address and the council's own records supply

options.text: A deadline, since the letter looks forward to a reply and sets no date for one

options.misconception: makes every reader a motorist, which one sentence does not require

options.text: That its readers attended the meeting or read its minutes, since no order is named
That its readers can read English well, since the notice is written in short sentences

options.misconception: invents a second expansion, which the notice's own sentence rules out

options.misconception: judges the sequence of a date, which is a reasonable thing to lead with

Users who have not completed the annual renewal will be offered a place on a waiting list.' What has the softened phrasing cost the reader?

The reason, since following the safety review invites a reader to go looking for it

options.text: The date, since from the start of next term is vaguer than a date would be
options.misconception: attacks a date the notice does give, in the terms the notice uses

options.text: The offer, since a place on a waiting list sounds like a place and is not one

questions.stem: A notice reads: 'NOTICE. The council has taken the decision to terminate the arrangement with the contractor on 30 June. options.text: Arrange, which is a bland word for what the contract actually is
options.misconception: objects to an ordinary noun, where the opinion is in the closing sentence

options.text: Regrets, which is an opinion none of the other three sentences carries
Interruption, which hints that service has been interrupted elsewhere before
options.misconception: reads a denial as a hint, where the sentence is reassuring

options.text: Terminate, which is a formal word for a decision a reader can grasp
options.misconception: objects to formality, which is a register choice and not a judgment

Arrangement, interruption and terminate are choices of register, and none of them adds a view.
questions.hint: Ask which word would have to be crossed out for the notice to say nothing more than it means.

questions.learningObjective: judge whether a summary can disclose more than the document it summarises

stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: Two documents say: 'The full report, paragraph 2: Names of the two staff involved in the error are given in this paragraph and appear nowhere else. The summary circulated to all staff: A review found that two members of staff made an error in the figures and both have since left the service.' Which sentence reports the relationship accurately?

options.text: The two agree, since a summary that omits the names is faithful to a report that withholds them
options.misconception: treats silence about a name as silence about everything connected with it

options.text: The summary is the fuller document, since it carries the finding and the outcome together
options.misconception: judges completeness by length rather than by what each document says

options.text: The report withholds the names and the summary discloses that both have left
The report is unusable, since a document that withholds names cannot be circulated at all
options.misconception: proposes a different circulation rule, which the passages do not discuss

questions.explanation: Compare the two documents by what each discloses, not by how much each contains. The full report names the two staff and says the names appear nowhere else; it says nothing about either person leaving. The summary omits the names, which is what the report's own rule would lead a writer to do, and adds that both have since left the service, which is a fact the report nowhere states. So the summary that was meant to be the safer document carries an item of news the fuller one does not, and a reader of the report alone would not know it. That is how a summary leaks, and it happens through what a careful writer adds rather than through what they leave out.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two documents contains a fact the other does not mention at all.

questions.topic: Confidentiality in a forwarded document
questions.learningObjective: judge what forwarding a document does to its limits

stimulus.body: The following is confidential to the named recipients and should not be passed on. Subject: staffing review. Two posts are at risk in the depot. The names are in the attached list, which is not for circulation outside the team. Please keep this to the team until the announcement on Thursday.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A message reads: 'The following is confidential to the named recipients and should not be passed on. Subject: staffing review. Two posts are at risk in the depot. The names are in the attached list, which is not for circulation outside the team. Please keep this to the team until the announcement on Thursday.' Which statement in it fails at the point most readers will test?

options.text: The rule not to pass the message on, since a forwarding reader will forward it regardless
options.misconception: treats a rule as the failure, where a rule is the only thing that can be repeated

options.text: The date of the announcement, since Thursday tells a reader when to expect the news
options.misconception: objects to a date, which a reader inside the team needs

options.text: The subject line, since staffing review tells a forwarder what the file is about
options.misconception: objects to a subject line, which is how a document is identified at all

options.text: The names are the sensitive part, while the two posts at risk can be retold

questions.explanation: Read the message for what a reader is likely to repeat. The names are protected, once, by an attached list that is not to circulate, and the existence of two posts at risk is stated in the body, in plain words, in a sentence that can be copied into a corridor or a group message without carrying the attachment with it. The document therefore treats the fact as less sensitive than the names, which is probably right, and protects it in the one place a reader is most likely to leak, which is not. A forwarding reader who obeys the rule keeps everything; a forwarding reader who ignores it loses everything. The message's real exposure is the sentence a reader can say without the attachment.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence a reader could repeat without breaking the rule the message sets.

questions.topic: A recommendation without a cost
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a recommendation has given the reader the price of acting
questions.stem: A brief recommends: 'We should move the market to the car park on the edge of town, where there is space for delivery vehicles and room to expand.' What has the recommendation not given the reader?

options.text: What the move would cost, since the case for it is made entirely in terms of space
Who currently uses the market, since the brief says nothing about the traders at all
options.misconception: asks for a stakeholder, which a one-line recommendation may leave to a fuller paper

options.text: How big the car park is, since the brief says there is room and no dimensions
options.misconception: asks for a measurement, when the gap is that no figure of any kind is given

options.text: Why the market is moving, since the brief begins with We should and gives no reason at all
options.misconception: misses that the two reasons given, space and room to expand, are the case

questions.explanation: The recommendation argues from two benefits, space for delivery vehicles and room to expand, and both are free words. A reader who is being asked to approve a move has to weigh them against what the move costs, and the brief offers nothing to weigh them against, not a figure for the works, not a rent, not a period over which the saving would come. That is the difference between recommending and proposing: a recommendation is a claim that the benefits outweigh the costs, and this one does not show the costs. The traders and the size of the car park are further questions, and the case is not missing, it is simply not priced.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is being asked to weigh the two stated benefits against.

The temporary signage will go up first so that the diversion is clear throughout. The new signs follow the design already agreed. This should be complete before the school term begins.' What has the note left open?

options.text: What the diversion is, since the note refers to it without describing the route
options.misconception: asks for a description, when the note's business is the order of the work

options.text: Who orders the signs and who takes the old ones away, since every task is a passive
How long the works take, since the note gives a date and no duration
options.misconception: asks for a duration, which a date before a fixed term already implies

options.text: What the design is, since the note says agreed and shows nothing at all
options.misconception: asks for the design, which is held in the document the note refers to

A reader of this note knows the order of the operations, which is the hard part, and not one person responsible for any of them, which is what an implementation note is asked for. questions.stem: A document map is printed as follows: 'DOCUMENT MAP, all in order as printed. Section 1: In this report, the depot means the building on Mill Lane. Section 2: The depot is to be sold, and the sale is expected to complete in the spring. Section 3: The depot's loading bays are to be relet to two businesses, one of which is the haulier currently using them. Section 4: Depot Road, which runs past the depot, will be closed for four weeks during the works. Section 5: The depot is to be demolished and the site used for a car park.' What has happened to the word depot across the document?

options.misconception: invents a second referent, which the map never introduces

options.text: It has been confused with a road, since section 4 places the two together in one sentence
options.misconception: reads a road name in a sentence about a building as a confusion

options.text: It has shifted from a building being sold to a site being cleared, without ever being redefined
It has stayed the same, since a building can be sold, relet and then demolished
options.misconception: accepts the sequence as one stable referent, and misses the change of thing described

Section 5 uses the same word for what remains after the building has gone, a site for a car park, and a site is not a building with loading bays, so the word has changed what it denotes without any sentence saying so. A reader who reads section 5 after section 3 has to decide whether a new thing has appeared or the old one has been described differently, and nothing in the map helps. Depot Road in section 4 is a different name, not a second sense.
questions.hint: Ask what the word denotes in section 1, in section 3, and in section 5.

questions.topic: An answer to an objection in a public comment
questions.learningObjective: judge whether an answer has met the objection it answers

stimulus.body: Some residents say the closure will be longer than six weeks. In fact the drainage works are scheduled for six weeks, and the contractor is engaged for that period. Six weeks is the figure in the contract and the council is not able to shorten it without a new agreement.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A response to objections runs: 'Some residents say the closure will be longer than six weeks. In fact the drainage works are scheduled for six weeks, and the contractor is engaged for that period. Six weeks is the figure in the contract and the council is not able to shorten it without a new agreement.' What has the response not done?

options.text: It has not given the date the works begin, since the response mentions six weeks and no starting point
options.misconception: asks for a start date, which the objection did not raise either

options.text: It has not explained what a resident should do if the works overrun, which is the fear behind the objection
It has not said who to contact, since the response ends without a name or a telephone number
options.misconception: asks for a contact detail, which is a matter for the covering letter

options.text: It has not admitted that overruns happen, since the response treats the schedule as certain
options.misconception: invents a concession the objection did not ask for

questions.explanation: Read the objection and the answer for what each is about. The objection is that the closure will last longer than six weeks, and the answer is that the works are scheduled for six weeks and cannot be shortened, which is a different question: a schedule is what is planned, and the resident's objection is about what happens when the plan slips. So the response answers the more comfortable half of the fear and leaves the half that would actually help a reader, which is what a resident does on the fourth week of a six-week job. Refusing to shorten a contract is a proper answer to half an objection.

When the works begin, since the record gives a cost and a contractor but no date

questions.topic: Order of the parts of an answer
questions.learningObjective: order the elements of an answer so it is usable by its reader
questions.stem: A clerk must answer a resident who asks whether the path will be open for the school visit. Put the four moves in the order the answer needs.

options.text: Say what the answer is based on, so the reader can weigh it if they doubt it
Say what is still not certain, so the reader knows what could change the answer
Say what the reader should do next, so the answer produces an action rather than a fact
Give the answer itself, so a reader who stops after one sentence knows where they stand

questions.explanation: An answer to a question is read by someone who wants to know where they stand, so the answer comes first and can be a whole sentence on its own. The basis comes second, and it is what lets a reader who doubts the answer say why; without it a confident answer can only be believed or ignored. What is uncertain comes third, because on a question about a date that is the part that decides whether the reader needs to do something now, and it is the part a careless answer leaves out. The action comes last, since it is what turns an answer into something the reader can use, and it cannot be written until the uncertainty has been stated.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs in order to act, and in what order each part of the answer reaches them.

The works are due to begin in September and to last about six weeks. Whether the diversion will be surfaced, and who pays for it, has not yet been decided and will come back to the committee.' options.misconception: reads the outstanding item as a sign of good practice in itself

options.text: Contradicted the first sentence, since an undecided item cannot sit in a decided matter
options.misconception: calls a deferred item a contradiction of the decision to proceed

options.text: Reopened a live part of the decision, so a reader who stops there cannot say the matter is settled
Given the reader more than they asked for, since nobody requested the state of the diversion
options.misconception: supposes a reader who has no interest in the diversion at all

questions.explanation: The record's first two sentences settle the matters a reader would most expect to be settled: that the works will happen, what they cost and when. The last sentence then hands back one of the consequences of that decision, the surface of the diversion and its cost, and the two are not independent, because a works timetable is hard to keep to a route that is under water. So a reader who reads to the end, which is the reader a record is written for, cannot tell whether the scheme as a whole is decided. Naming the outstanding item is right; leaving it as the record's last word, attached to a decision already taken, is what reopens the question.
questions.hint: Ask whether the outstanding item can be settled on its own, or whether it affects the decision above it.

questions.topic: A sign-off that promises action
questions.learningObjective: judge what a closing courtesy costs a reader
questions.stem: A message ends: 'Thanks in advance for your help with this. I look forward to hearing from you.' What do those two sentences do for a reader?

options.text: They commit the writer to a reply, since hearing from you promises an answer
options.misconception: reads a courteous hope as a undertaking the writer has taken on

options.text: They make the request more pressing, since politeness signals that the matter is urgent
options.misconception: attributes urgency to politeness, which carries no information about timing

options.text: They show the writer is junior, since asking for help is something a junior member does
options.misconception: reads rank into a courtesy, which the two sentences do not signal

options.text: They close warmly and add nothing, since neither says what is wanted or by when

Neither says what is wanted, by when, or what will happen if the reader does nothing, so a reader who reads only the closing has nothing to act on, and the request itself is left wherever the message put it. That is not a fault of manner; it is the cost of a close that carries no content. A hope of a reply is not a promise of one, courtesy says nothing about urgency, and asking for help says nothing about anyone's position.

Suppliers should note that deliveries to the bays after April need a booked slot, and the booking form is attached.' Which sentence reports the note accurately?

options.misconception: supplies a rule about circulation that the note's own arrangement contradicts

options.misconception: makes neutrality a meaning of assessment, when an assessment is a weighing

options.misconception: asks for a second document's contents, where a decision record is one decision

options.text: The decision itself, in words close to those the committee used

The decision in the committee's own words, because a paraphrase in a record loses the qualifications that were part of the vote. The basis, because a decision without its ground cannot be revisited, only obeyed or ignored, and a later reader who disagrees needs to know what they are disagreeing with. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A weak sentence in a draft
questions.learningObjective: say what a sentence has to carry and rewrite it to carry it
questions.stem: A draft of a committee paper contains: 'It is important to note that the delay which was caused by the issue with the supplier was, in the circumstances, somewhat disappointing.' In three or four sentences, say what this sentence has to do to be worth keeping, and rewrite it.

answer.exemplar: The sentence has to tell the reader who was delayed, by what, and what the delay costs them, and to say it in as few words as will carry all three. As printed it delivers none of them: the actor is a passive, the cause is a chain of nouns with no agent, the delay has no length, and the opinion at the end, somewhat disappointing, tells a reader nothing they could not have assumed. A version that carries the three facts is: 'The supplier missed the delivery date, so the fence cannot be completed before the school term begins.' That says who is responsible, what the delay is, and what it costs the reader, and it leaves out the judgment, because the cost is already in the sentence.

questions.explanation: A committee paper earns a sentence by the information the reader needs and cannot get elsewhere, and this one is almost entirely made of framing. It is important to note and in the circumstances are both phrases that tell a reader the writer is about to say something; somewhat disappointing is a judgment that adds nothing the facts will not show better; the delay, the issue and the supplier are all given as nouns in a chain, so nobody in the sentence does anything. The rewrite has to be tested against one question, which of these would a reader lose if the sentence were gone. The exemplar supplies a version that loses nothing, and a good answer will keep the real content and drop the framing rather than tidy the framing.

Of those, forty-one said they would use it more often if it were surfaced, and twenty-one said they would not. options.misconception: supplies a different question, where the sentence's own claim is about support

options.text: Forty-one is not a majority, since a majority of 120 needs sixty-one households to agree

options.misconception: attacks the sampling frame, which the sentence does not rely on

options.text: The replies are counted as the people affected, when 58 of the 120 households never answered

questions.explanation: The last sentence says the scheme is supported by a clear majority of the people affected, and the report's own figures say the people affected are 120 households. Forty-one is a clear majority of the sixty-two who replied and a minority of the hundred and twenty who were asked, so the sentence's subject, the people affected, and the report's evidence, the people who replied, are not the same group. That is the strongest objection, because it is a matter of which population a count is being used to represent, and no further evidence is needed to establish it. A different question, a different sampling frame, and an arithmetic objection that ignores which base the report uses each are all weaker than the one the report's own sentence supplies.
questions.hint: Ask how many households the report counts as the people affected, and how many the figure comes from.
